Naive Bayes — Easy → Formal

Core Idea
Naive Bayes is a probabilistic classifier based on Bayes' Theorem:

  P(Class | Features) ∝ P(Features | Class) × P(Class)

"Naive" assumption: all features are independent of each other given the class.

Example — Email Spam Detection
Training set: 60 spam, 140 ham (200 total)
Vocabulary: {buy, free, offer, meeting}

          buy  free  offer  meeting
Spam(60):  45    50    40       5
Ham(140):  10     8    12     120

P(spam) = 60/200 = 0.30
P(ham)  = 140/200 = 0.70

Classify new email: "buy free"
P(spam|"buy free") ∝ (45/60) × (50/60) × 0.30 = 0.1875
P(ham |"buy free") ∝ (10/140) × (8/140) × 0.70 = 0.00284
→ SPAM ✓

Formal Definitions (from your image)
Multinomial NB:
  θ_{w,c} = n_{w,c} / n_c
  where n_{w,c} = count of word w in class c, n_c = total words in class c

Gaussian NB (continuous features):
  P(x_i|c) = (1/√(2πσ²_ic)) × exp(-(x_i - μ_ic)² / 2σ²_ic)

Prediction:
  ŷ = argmax_c [ log P(c) + Σ_i log P(x_i|c) ]  ← use log-sum to avoid underflow
I am not understanding what u dios in Test: "buy free"... It kills everything because of zero probability

You caught the critical Zero Probability Problem — good catch!

The Problem
If the word "free" never appeared in spam training data:
  n_{free, spam} = 0
  P(free | spam) = 0/60 = 0

Then:
  P(spam | "buy free") ∝ P(buy|spam) × 0 × P(spam) = 0

The entire probability collapses to zero — even "buy" (a strong spam signal) is killed.

Solution: Laplace (Add-1) Smoothing
Add pseudocount α=1 to every word:

  θ_{w,c} = (n_{w,c} + 1) / (n_c + |V|)

Where |V| = vocabulary size.

With α=1, |V|=4, even if "free" = 0 in spam:
  P(free|spam) = (0 + 1)/(60 + 4) = 1/64 ≠ 0

Now multiplication never collapses. Every word gets a small non-zero baseline.

Rendering issue — LaTeX symbols not showing. Plain text version:

Multinomial NB parameter estimation (plain text):

  P(word_w | class_c) = (count(w in c) + alpha) / (total_words_in_c + alpha * vocab_size)

  Prior: P(class_c) = (docs in class c) / (total docs)

Gaussian NB parameter estimation (plain text):

  Mean:     mu[c,i]     = (1/n_c) * SUM of x_i for all samples in class c
  Variance: sigma2[c,i] = (1/n_c) * SUM of (x_i - mu[c,i])^2 for all samples in class c

  Likelihood: P(x_i|c) = (1/sqrt(2*pi*sigma2)) * exp(-(x_i-mu)^2 / (2*sigma2))

Prediction (log form to avoid underflow):
  log P(c|x) = log P(c) + SUM_i [ log P(x_i|c) ]

SVM + Kernels + SMO — Complete (nothing skipped)

PART 1: SVM Core
Goal: Find hyperplane w·x + b = 0 that maximizes margin = 2/||w||

Primal (hard-margin):
  Minimize: (1/2)||w||²
  Subject to: y_i(w·x_i + b) ≥ 1 for all i

Soft-margin (with slack ξ_i):
  Minimize: (1/2)||w||² + C·Σξ_i
  Subject to: y_i(w·x_i + b) ≥ 1 - ξ_i,  ξ_i ≥ 0

PART 2: Dual Formulation
Using Lagrange multipliers α_i:
  Maximize: W(α) = Σα_i - (1/2) Σ_i Σ_j α_i α_j y_i y_j (x_i·x_j)
  Subject to: 0 ≤ α_i ≤ C  and  Σ α_i y_i = 0

Key: dual only uses dot products x_i·x_j → replace with kernel K(x_i, x_j)

PART 3: Kernels + Mercer's Condition (from your image)
Linear:     K(x,z) = x·z
Polynomial: K(x,z) = (x·z + c)^d
RBF:        K(x,z) = exp(-||x-z||²/(2σ²))

Mercer's Condition: K is a valid kernel iff the kernel matrix K_ij = K(x_i,x_j) is positive semi-definite.
PSD means: for any vector v,  v^T K v ≥ 0  (all eigenvalues ≥ 0).

PART 4: SMO Algorithm
Problem: Solving dual with N variables simultaneously is expensive.

SMO idea: pick 2 multipliers α_i, α_j that violate KKT conditions most. Fix all others. Solve 2-variable subproblem analytically.

Why 2? Constraint Σ α_i y_i = 0 couples all variables — you need at least 2 free at once.

Update rules:
  α₂_new = α₂_old + y₂(E₁ - E₂)/η
  where η = 2K(x₁,x₂) - K(x₁,x₁) - K(x₂,x₂)
  and E_i = f(x_i) - y_i  (prediction error)

  Clip α₂ to [L, H] to satisfy 0 ≤ α ≤ C
  Then α₁ = α₁_old + y₁y₂(α₂_old - α₂_new)

Bias b updated after each pair to restore KKT.

explain continuous variable discretization for naive bayes
[uploaded image: textbook section on equal-width and equal-frequency binning with interval examples]

Continuous Variable Discretization for Naive Bayes

Problem: Multinomial NB expects discrete (count) features. But features like height=175.3, age=23.7 are continuous.

Two options:
1. Use Gaussian NB directly (model with μ, σ² per feature per class) — no discretization needed.
2. Discretize first → then apply Multinomial NB.

Equal-Width Binning (from your image):
  bin_width = (max - min) / k
  Bins: [min, min+w), [min+w, min+2w), ..., [max-w, max]

  Example: ages {18,22,35,45,60,72}, k=3
  width = (72-18)/3 = 18
  Bin 1 [18,36) → "young"
  Bin 2 [36,54) → "middle"
  Bin 3 [54,72] → "senior"

Equal-Frequency (Quantile) Binning:
  Each bin holds equal number of samples.
  Better for skewed distributions (equal-width leaves some bins empty).

After discretization: replace each value with bin label, treat as categorical.

Trade-off: more bins → less info loss, more sparsity; fewer bins → smoother but loses signal.
Typical practice: 5-10 bins.

[uploaded image: Bias-Variance tradeoff graph — U-shaped total error curve, bias² decreasing left-to-right, variance increasing left-to-right]
explain this graph

Bias-Variance Tradeoff Graph

Axes:
  X: Model complexity (left = simple, right = complex)
  Y: Prediction error

Three curves:
1. Bias² — decreases as complexity increases
   High bias = model too simple → systematic wrong assumptions
   E.g., fitting a line to curved data → always wrong in the same direction

2. Variance — increases as complexity increases
   High variance = model memorizes training noise → overfits
   E.g., degree-15 polynomial fits training perfectly, fails on test

3. Total Error = Bias² + Variance + σ²_irreducible
   U-shaped curve. Bottom of U = optimal model complexity.

Practical rules:
  Left of U (underfitting): add features, increase complexity, less regularization
  Right of U (overfitting): L1/L2 regularization, more data, simpler model

Key formula:
  Expected MSE = Bias² + Variance + σ²

Exam one-liner: High bias → underfits (too simple). High variance → overfits (too complex). Minimize both to generalize.
